We delineate four paradigms: STING activation upstream induces phagocytosis in lung inflammation, sepsis, spinal cord injury, cancer, and viral infection; phagocytosis initiates STING by delivering immunogenic cargo; positive feedback loops amplify antitumor immunity; and STING can suppress phagocytosis in obesity-driven adipose inflammation. Importantly, this axis exerts opposing regulatory effects across disease settings, being protective or pathogenic, synergistic or antagonistic, depending on cell type, stimulus, and pathological context. We further synthesize advanced nanoplatforms-biomimetic nanoparticles, hybrid membrane vesicles, DNA nanodevices, lymph node-targeted nanovaccines, and "Trojan horse" nanocapsules-engineered to co-deliver STING agonists, phagocytosis checkpoint inhibitors, and immunogenic cargo. These nanotherapies enhance antitumor and antimicrobial defense, resolve inflammation, and overcome barriers such as the blood-brain barrier. By integrating mechanism with nanobiotechnology, this review provides a conceptual framework for the cGAS -STING-phagocytosis network and a roadmap for next-generation nanomedicines treating cancer, infection, neurodegeneration, and inflammatory disorders.

title: Periprosthetic Joint Infection Caused by Streptococcus equi Subspecies zooepidemicus: The First Reported Case Confirmed by Synovial Fluid Culture.
abstract: Streptococcus equi subspecies zooepidemicus (SEZ) is a pathogen associated with infections in horses. It can occasionally transmit and cause clinical infections in humans. Even though the bacterium is an opportunistic pathogen, human infections are often severe such as meningitis, septicemia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis. We report a unique case of synovial fluid culture-confirmed periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) caused by SEZ. The patient had undergone a total knee arthroplasty due to osteoarthritis. Five months postoperatively, she was admitted to the hospital with fever and clinical signs of PJI of the knee. The bacterial culture of the synovial fluid and blood cultures revealed SEZ. The 16S rRNA polymerase chain reaction (16S rRNA PCR) and culture of perioperative synovial tissue samples confirmed the same bacterium. Within 48 h of the onset of PJI symptoms, an operation with DAIR (debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention) was performed and followed by 12 weeks of antibiotic therapy. The prosthetic joint was preserved, and the patient had fully recovered with no signs of infection relapse at the 2-year follow-up. Two weeks prior to the PJI symptoms, the patient had visited a horse stable, where one of the horses had symptoms of an upper respiratory infection. We present the first case of synovial fluid culture-confirmed PJI caused by SEZ described in the literature. SEZ can be transmitted from horses to humans and cause serious infections, including PJI. The bacterium should be kept in mind when investigating acute infections, including PJI, in people who encounter horses due to their profession or hobbies.

title: Humoral immune responses and adverse effects of inactivated West Nile virus and tetanus toxoid vaccines administered via the subcutaneous or intramuscular route in horses.
abstract: Myosin heavy chain myopathy (MYHM) is a genetic disorder in Quarter Horse-related breeds that can result in non-exertional rhabdomyolysis and immune-mediated myositis. Infectious diseases and muscle damage, particularly from intramuscular (IM) vaccination, have been implicated as potential triggers for this condition. However, the subcutaneous (SC) injection route has not been investigated as an alternative vaccination method for MYHM-affected horses. The hypothesis was that there would be no difference in humoral immune responses or injection site reactions in healthy horses receiving killed West Nile virus (WNV) and tetanus toxoid vaccines via SC and IM routes. The primary objective was to determine serum antibody titers and the adverse effects elicited by both vaccination routes. A randomized, single-blind, two-arm, two-period study compared the responses in horses receiving WNV and tetanus vaccines via IM or SC routes. A total of 17 adult mares, all of which were negative for the MYH1 mutation, from a university research and teaching herd were included in the study. Serum antibody levels were assessed on the day of each vaccination. Antibody levels were also assessed on days 28 and 56 after WNV vaccine and on day 28 after tetanus toxoid administration. Vaccine site reactions were assessed daily for 72 h after vaccination. Antibody levels and injection site reactions were analyzed using two-way repeated measures ANOVA, rank sum tests, and Fisher's exact test, with statistical significance at a p-value of <0.05. Serum neutralization antibody titers increased after WNV vaccination regardless of the route of vaccine administration (p = 0.007), with no differences observed between routes of administration. Injection site swelling was greater after SC vaccination than after IM injection route for the WNV vaccine (p = 0.003). Baseline tetanus titers were high in almost all horses, and no change in titer was observed following vaccination. Injection site swelling was greater after SC tetanus vaccination than after IM vaccination (p = 0.002). Subcutaneous vaccination was associated with significant local reactions. An accurate assessment of humoral responses was challenging as the horses included in the study had high baseline titers from previous vaccinations. As a result, drawing definitive conclusions regarding the equivalence of responses to SC versus IM vaccination is difficult. Therefore, the results regarding this comparison must be considered inconclusive.

title: Sustainability stories in Swedish riding schools: an ecolinguistic analysis of policy documents and interviews.
journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
abstract: The equine sector provides employment opportunities and leisure activities for a substantial number of people in Sweden. Although these activities are closely connected to nature and dependent on ecosystem services, the sector faces significant ecological challenges. This article explores how representatives of the equine sector-particularly riding schools-conceptualize and articulate their work with environmental sustainability in policy documents and "talk about" everyday practice. The analysis is informed by the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and grounded in an ecolinguistic framework. Our results show that national level policy documents are closely aligned with the established sustainability terminology, whereas local documents and interviewees rarely employ SDG related terminology. Despite this discursive distance, riding schools demonstrate strong engagement and considerable creativity in addressing local environmental challenges. However, this ambition is constrained by limited knowledge, resources, and authority to address more complex ecological issues. Within the pedagogical environments that riding schools constitute, systematic instruction on environmental sustainability holds a marginal position. We identified five "stories we live by": "the responsible local care taker", "we try, but we lack resources", "learning through everyday practice", "sustainability without sustainability terminology" and "small action matters". We have interpreted this as emerging eco-benifical narratives that can carry pedagogical potential. We argue that with strengthened organizational support, clearer conceptual tools, and structured opportunities for capacity building, riding schools could play a more active role in shaping sustainability-oriented "stories to live by" and contribute more fully to the broader societal transition toward sustainable development.

title: Comparative study of in vitro digestibility and antioxidant activities of whey from different milks.
abstract: Whey proteins, a protein-rich by-product of milk, contribute to various biological benefits. These bioactivities play an important role in human health and can be enhanced when whey proteins are digested, yet the digestion of whey proteins from different animal species under standardized protocols of in vitro digestion and its effect on antioxidant activity remain insufficiently characterized. This work aims to compare the digestibility and antioxidant activities of whey from the milk of different animal species: cameline, bovine, ovine, caprine, and equine. Milk samples from the five species were coagulated to obtain whey. The whey proteins were digested with pepsin and pancreatin in an in vitro process that mimics digestion in the gastrointestinal tract. Physicochemical parameters, protein profiles (SDS‑PAGE), peptide concentration, degree of hydrolysis (DH), and antioxidant activities were analyzed to assess inter‑species differences. After milk coagulation, a slight increase in pH values was observed in all whey samples. The maximum peptide concentration was observed in the digested ewe whey, while digested mare whey showed the lowest. Camel whey has the highest content of sodium, potassium, zinc and iron, while goat whey has the highest concentration of copper and ewe whey has the highest concentration of calcium. The SDS-PAGE profiles showed that all five milk types had an identical protein profile, with the exception of camel whey, which was characterised by the absence of β-lactoglobulin (β-Lg) and the presence of two different proteins camel whey basic protein (CWBP) and Peptidoglycan recognition protein (PGRP). The highest antioxidant activity was found in ewe whey. The sensitivity of whey proteins to hydrolysis varies between milk types. Correlation analysis indicated that the DH was significantly positively correlated with peptide concentrations (r = 0.998, p < 0.0001), indicating that increased proteolysis facilitates peptide liberation. Simulated gastrointestinal digestion produced peptides exhibiting antioxidant properties across all five species, reinforcing the notion that whey hydrolysates offer a valuable avenue for enhancing this by-product. These findings highlight the nutritional and functional diversity of whey proteins among animal species. Hydrolysates of whey proteins from all animal species studied could be an interesting approach to add value to this by-product.

title: Anatomical and computed tomographic study of equine cervical spinal nerves and intervertebral foramina.
abstract: Osseous enlargement of the cervical articular process joints due to osteoarthropathy or developmental hypertrophy can narrow the intervertebral foramen (IF), resulting in compression and neuritis of the exiting spinal nerves. Associated clinical signs may include neck pain, forelimb lameness or muscle atrophy. Computed tomography (CT) is the gold standard for IF evaluation; however, to date, visualisation of the equine spinal nerves based on CT imaging is insufficient. To improve the diagnostic accuracy of foraminal stenosis and cervical spinal nerve (CSN) compression based on CT, this study aims to describe the anatomical size and position of the CSN at the level of the IF. Cadaveric study. Anatomical dissection was performed to expose the dorsal and ventral rami of CSN3-CSN8 in 10 cervical specimens (n = 88 IF and CSN). Barium sulfate was applied to the nerves, and CT imaging was performed. The cross-sectional area (CSA) of the IF and CSN, the CSN shape and position within the foramen were quantified. Both IF and CSN CSA significantly increased caudally, with the largest values identified at C7-Th1. The ratio of the spinal nerves CSA to IF CSA was significantly higher caudally, suggesting a greater risk of compression in this region. The CSN position within the IF varied between vertebral levels and was positioned in the mid-caudal third of the IF between C3 and C6 and more cranial in the IFs between C6 and Th1. Ex vivo character of the study and the relatively small sample size. These findings demonstrate significant anatomical variation in the size, shape and position of the CSN inside the IF depending on the vertebral level. Detailed knowledge of these patterns enables increased diagnostic precision and the development of targeted therapeutic interventions in equine CSN compression.
